edits.old: Instantiating the supplied coherent sampler at $q$ repetitions gives $qk$ abstract reads; its generic compiler uses at most $2qk$ physical bit queries. The complete Lemma 2.1(ii) wrapper packages this construction with a repetition count $n$ and law existentially quantified; its proof chooses $n=q$. It binds one isometry $F_z$, one initial basis state, one output labeling, and that isometry's measured law. The physical implementation applies the same $F_z$ before every subsequent continuation and adds at most $2nk$ to the continuation's cap. This connects coherence, the measured law, and the physical cost in one witness, proving the required $O_k(1+\log(1/\eta))$ conclusion. The explicit ceiling choice is supplied by the repetition and decoder theorems, rather than asserted by the wrapper's existential statement alone.

During the next transform, a partial butterfly sum has at most $m$ terms, each bounded by $m^j$, so its magnitude is at most $m^{j+1}$. Sign changes preserve these bounds. edits.old: The direct proof constructs two distributions on the whole sign cube. The first is uniform. The second is obtained by rounding a chain of correlated Gaussian vectors to signs. Their Forrelation means differ, but a shallow decision tree has nearly the same expectation under both distributions. To prove this indistinguishability, scale only the first block of Gaussian biases. Differentiation starts in that block; Gaussian integration by parts then moves the derivative through one coordinate of each successive block. Every attempted return to a coordinate already differentiated vanishes by multilinearity. The resulting order-$k$ derivative sum is controlled by a martingale along the decision tree.

edits.old: A winning column must do two things: contain an all-one string, and supply a zero in every other column. Its zero witnesses are stored in a cell whose address is determined by several partial-function values. Transcripts in that cell certify that these values are defined and that the proposed address is correct. This gives a total predicate even when many of the partial-function instances lie outside their promise. The outward direction of the pointers also makes the winner safe against an opponent whose decoded address is meaningless: every pointer into the winner still reaches a one.

At the first gate, each predecessor is an input or a constant, so the claimed output equals the evaluated output. Suppose this has been proved for every earlier gate. Each predecessor of the next gate then has its evaluated value, and that gate's equation forces its claimed output to have its evaluated value too. Induction proves equality at every gate. This proof holds for inputs outside $D$, since $C$ is a total circuit. In particular, every input has exactly one gate-consistent transcript. ∎

edits.old: **Proof and query count.** For each test, use its decision tree from (4.13). At every level, retain the earlier answers and compute the next queried location by an input-independent reversible operation. The location can depend on those retained answers: this is how the pointer lookup works. Query into a fresh answer register and retain enough history to make each update reversible. A leaf determines the test output exactly. Pad shorter branches to the common depth $q_*$ with inactive reads. A controlled bit read can be implemented with two ordinary oracle calls: load the bit into a temporary register, use it conditionally, and query again to clear the temporary register.

edits.old: Uniform-index evaluation is a particular use of (4.15). Prepare the input-independent state $K^{-1/2}\sum_e|e\rangle$ and run the controlled evaluator. If $h$ tests fail, the probability of observing a failed test is $h/K$, because the index blocks are orthogonal and each test is exact. Thus all tests passing gives failure-detection probability zero, while a nonwinner at any proposed address gives probability at least $1/K$. The later search routine uses the evaluator and its inverse with the retained work registers. A theorem only about this uniform distribution would not, by itself, supply the arbitrary-index action (4.15).

edits.old: The algorithm first produces a short list likely to contain the winning column, then checks the listed columns. Its central calculation is a drift identity: complementary comparison probabilities make the total surviving weight fall by at least half in expectation, while a true winner retains almost all its weight until it is selected. This works even if the other columns compare cyclically or have meaningless decoded addresses. Exact local verification subsequently rejects incorrect certificates. Both the search and the verification have a fixed query cap on every input, including inputs outside all the partial-function promises.

edits.old: A coherent implementation may run all $N$ trial registers and then route the first success, which keeps the same padded cap. It needs no controlled access to an otherwise opaque preparation unitary. To control a Grover iterate, apply $A$ and $A^{-1}$ unconditionally, control only the fixed reflections $S_0,S_\chi$, and apply the minus sign as a phase on the true control. On a false control the reflections are identities and $AA^{-1}=I$; on a true control the operation is $G$. The iteration-count record therefore controls only input-independent gates. Equality of label distributions alone would be insufficient. Write $|\pm\rangle=(|0\rangle\pm|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$. The vectors
$$
 |+\rangle\otimes|0\rangle
 \quad\hbox{and}\quad
 \frac{|0\rangle|0\rangle+|1\rangle|1\rangle}{\sqrt2}
$$
give the same uniform computational-basis distribution on the first register. In the first vector that register is pure $|+\rangle$; in the second it has density matrix $I/2$. Measuring it in the $\{|+\rangle,|-\rangle\}$ basis distinguishes the two laws: the probability of $+$ is respectively $1$ and $1/2$. This elementary example explains why the formal successful-label theorem cannot by itself certify the full successful-state assertion. It does not contradict the ordinary proof of Lemma 3.1 just given.

edits.old: Høyer, Mosca and de Wolf [HMW2003, arXiv v2, §1, pp. 1–3, and §3, pp. 4–7] study search when each underlying Boolean predicate is computed correctly with probability at least $9/10$. edits.old: Reading a pointer requires its $\ell$ address bits, followed by the targeted $X$-bit. Reversible reading keeps the pointer and the target address available for uncomputation. Thus the two pointer tests use $O(\ell+1)$ bit queries, with a constant factor if controlled reads are needed. edits.old: For `claim-comparison-state`, we check why the coherent calculation has the probabilities suggested by the classical description. After decoding, write the state as a sum over the two decoded labels, with every summand carrying those labels in dedicated retained registers. The subsequent pointer tests and winner computation are controlled by these labels and do not erase them. The final projection onto a winning output is block diagonal with respect to the retained labels. Thus the squared norm of that projection is the sum, over label pairs, of the squared norms of the corresponding projected summands. Cross terms vanish because distinct labels are orthogonal. Within one summand, the pointer test reads the designated bits. Its contribution is therefore the decoding probability of those labels multiplied by the deterministic result of the comparison rule at those labels.

Computing the coordinate from already stored labels is an input-independent reversible operation, so it costs no query. A pointer is stored in $\ell$ separate input bits, and reading them, reversibly forming the indicated coordinate, and querying that coordinate costs $\ell+1$ ordinary queries before any uncomputation.

edits.old: A controlled read can always be implemented with two ordinary bit queries. Start with a fresh answer ancilla zero. Query $x_u$ into that ancilla, perform the desired action controlled jointly by its value and by the original control, and query $x_u$ again to erase the ancilla. Keep the coordinate $u$ unchanged until this second query. The desired action can be an XOR into an output register or a sign change. The resulting transformation is the controlled bit or phase query on every superposition of $u$, control, and workspace, because the basis-state calculation applies linearly. The same construction works when the original control is false: both queries still occur, and their effects cancel.

edits.old: An exact adaptive local test can be made coherent by retaining its previous query answers, using them to compute the next coordinate, and padding its computation to the fixed maximum depth. At a branch that has halted early, the remaining controlled reads are disabled. Every gate remains a fixed function of the retained labels. The query count is at most a constant times the decision-tree depth. Reversing the full circuit gives the inverse with the same cost. These operations justify coherent comparisons, their inverses, uniform local-test preparation, and the reflections used by amplification within the ordinary bit-oracle model.

edits.old: The source provides a concrete compilation argument behind this accounting. An abstract read has a coordinate function on basis labels, an involutive permutation of those labels, and an optional sign. Applying that permutation does not change either its coordinate or its sign. Given a basis label, the compiler embeds the abstract register into the physical coordinate, answer-bit, and workspace registers, loads the queried bit, applies the indicated signed permutation if that bit is one, queries the unchanged coordinate again, and returns to the chosen embedding. On bit zero it is the identity; on bit one it is exactly the prescribed signed involution. Both actions preserve inner products. The finite isometries used to place the active register extend to unitaries on sufficiently large finite workspace by completing an orthonormal basis. This is why no unmentioned input-dependent gate is needed.

edits.old: Composing these read implementations adds their caps, and reversing their logical circuit uses the same number of reads. A circuit of $q$ logical reads is consequently implemented with at most $2q$ ordinary bit queries, also when its indices are superposed. For classical-label continuations, one may measure the complete computational-basis state and then apply a basis permutation taking the known outcome back to the fixed initial basis state. This reset has no query cost. Its classical output law is exact, but the measurement is not an implementation of returning an unmeasured original quantum state. This distinction explains the two amplification interfaces discussed in Appendix G.7.

edits.old: The older Boolean continuation runs the tournament and then verifies the listed candidates, returning one acceptance bit instead of a list. We give its induction, so the difference in its statement has a complete mathematical explanation. Fix verifier acceptance probabilities $v(i)\in[0,1]$, and let $V(L)$ be the probability that at least one fresh verification of a member of $L$ accepts. Sequential verification gives $V([])=0$ and $V(i::L)=v(i)+(1-v(i))V(L)$. In particular $0\leq V(L)\leq1$; if $s\in L$, then $V(L)\geq v(s)$; and if all $v(i)\leq\varepsilon$, then $V(L)\leq|L|\varepsilon$. Each assertion follows by induction on the list using the recursive rule, or equivalently by the union bound for the verifier outcomes.

edits.old: Let $R_n(L)$ be the acceptance probability with $n$ tournament stages still available after history $L$. With no stage remaining it is $V(L)$. With a stage remaining, it is the sum of $f(L)V(L)$, representing immediate sampler failure and verification of the present list, and $(1-f(L))\sum_i(w_i/W)R_{n-1}(i::L)$, representing a successful pivot and continuation. When $W=0$, set the weighted sum to zero; the guaranteed $f(L)=1$ makes the same formula correct. For positive $W$, the weights in that sum are nonnegative and sum to one. It follows inductively that $R_n(L)\in[0,1]$. If all $v(i)\leq\varepsilon$, the same recursion gives $R_n(L)\leq(|L|+n)\varepsilon$: an immediate stop has bound $|L|\varepsilon$, and each successful successor has bound $(|L|+1+n-1)\varepsilon$. A convex combination preserves the larger bound.

When $W=0$ we set the weighted sum to zero, and the guaranteed $f(L)=1$ makes the same formula correct; for positive $W$, the weights in that sum are nonnegative and sum to one. It follows inductively that $R_n(L)\in[0,1]$. If all $v(i)\leq\varepsilon$, the same recursion gives $R_n(L)\leq(|L|+n)\varepsilon$, because an immediate stop has bound $|L|\varepsilon$, each successful successor has bound $(|L|+1+n-1)\varepsilon$, and a convex combination preserves the larger bound.

Averaging the inductive lower bounds at successors gives a lower bound $Q=(1-\varepsilon)(1-I_n(L)-(n-1)\varepsilon)$ for the successful continuation. This proves the induction without assuming that failure probabilities at different histories are equal or independent.

one-input continuation values.

in all the finite averages below. Repeating a consistent answer leaves the
constraint set unchanged, although it still spends a query.

Induction proves that $W_c(\nu)$ is exactly the maximum weighted success
of a tree of depth at most $c$. At depth zero the two constants are the
only choices. At the next depth, each displayed candidate is attained by
an old optimal tree or by a query followed by two optimal smaller trees.
Conversely, every tree is a constant or starts with some query $a$; splitting
its success sum by that answer bounds it by the corresponding candidate.
This proves both directions. In particular, $W_c$ is nonnegative and
nondecreasing in $c$, and the two branch values with one fewer query sum
to at most the old value. A nonnegative weight of mass zero vanishes
pointwise, so all its success values are zero.
